Key 1–c, 2–a, 3–b (option 2). In Politics, Book III, Aristotle uses two tests: how many rule (one, few, many) and in whose interest. Rule by one for the common good is monarchy, for the ruler's own good tyranny; rule by a few virtuous people is aristocracy, by a few wealthy in their own interest oligarchy; rule by the many for the common good is polity, by the many poor in their own interest 'democracy'. Trap: Aristotle used 'democracy' for a perverted form, unlike its modern positive sense; India's Preamble ('Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic') uses the modern sense. Option 1 pairs monarchy with oligarchy, which is a rule of the few; option 3 pairs aristocracy (few) with democracy (many); option 4 pairs monarchy (one) with democracy. Revise with card 6.1.2-C01 (table POL-612-classification-axes).

facts.claim: Key 1–c, 2–d, 3–a, 4–b (option 1). Plato discussed the ideal State ruled by philosopher-kings in the Republic, and forms of government again in the Statesman and the Laws. His pupil Aristotle classified constitutions in the Politics. Thomas Hobbes argued in Leviathan (1651) for an absolute sovereign set up by a social contract. John Locke's Two Treatises of Government (1689) defended limited government based on consent, with natural rights to life, liberty and property; this tradition of limited government underlies written constitutions such as the US Constitution and the rights in Part III of the Indian Constitution. Option 2 swaps Plato and Aristotle; option 3 swaps Hobbes and Locke; option 4 swaps both pairs. Revise with card 6.1.2-C01 (table POL-612-classification-axes).
